\section{Independent Sets Cliques}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.IndependentSetsCliques.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{definition}[A covering $K$: every edge has an end in $K$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCovering}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCovering}
\leanok
A set of vertices touching every edge.  Theorem 7.1 says coverings and
independent sets are exactly complementary.

\textbf{!} Duplicated from \texttt{Matchings.lean}, textually identical.  Neither file imports the
other; see \texttt{log/graphtheory-ISSUES.md} \S{}F.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[isIndepSet_iff_isCovering_compl]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isIndepSet_iff_isCovering_compl}
\label{SimpleGraph.isIndepSet_iff_isCovering_compl}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCovering}
$V \ S$ is $S^{c}$.  Independent sets and coverings are complementary, which is why
the book's figure 7.1 shows independent sets visibly complementing coverings.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The covering number $\beta(G)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.coveringNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.coveringNumber}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCovering}
The fewest vertices touching every edge.  $\alpha$ is Mathlib's \texttt{indepNum}; only $\beta$
needs defining here.

\textbf{+} No \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} pitfall: \texttt{Set.univ} is always a covering, so the set being
minimised is never empty.  Contrast \texttt{edgeCoveringNumber} below, where the trap is
live.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[indepNum_add_coveringNumber]
\lean{SimpleGraph.indepNum_add_coveringNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.indepNum_add_coveringNumber}
\uses{SimpleGraph.coveringNumber}
The largest independent set and the smallest covering are exact complements:
choosing one is the same problem as choosing the other.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The matching number $\alpha'(G)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.matchingNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.matchingNumber}
\leanok
An \texttt{sSup} over matching sizes --- the edge analogue of $\alpha$.  Bounded above by
$\varepsilon$, so the supremum is attained; as with \texttt{coveringNumber} that attainment is not
packaged and must be re-derived at each use.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[An edge covering $L$: every vertex is an end of some edge of $L$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCovering}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCovering}
\leanok
A set of edges touching every vertex.  The \texttt{L $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet} conjunct is the book's
"subset of $E$", which matters here --- without it $L$ could contain non-edges and
cover trivially.

The existence caveat is what forces the $\delta > 0$ hypothesis on Theorem 7.2; see
\texttt{edgeCoveringNumber} below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The edge covering number $\beta'(G)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeCoveringNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeCoveringNumber}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCovering}
The fewest edges touching every vertex.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap here}, unlike \texttt{coveringNumber}.  When $\delta = 0$ no
edge covering exists, the set being minimised is empty, and Lean's convention
silently returns $0$ --- a value the book would call undefined.  That is precisely
why Theorem 7.2 carries $\delta > 0$, and why any lemma about $\beta'$ must either assume
it or handle the degenerate case explicitly.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[matchingNumber_add_edgeCoveringNumber]
\lean{SimpleGraph.matchingNumber_add_edgeCoveringNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.matchingNumber_add_edgeCoveringNumber}
\uses{SimpleGraph.edgeCoveringNumber, SimpleGraph.matchingNumber}
The striking parallel with Corollary 7.1 --- even though matchings and edge
coverings are \textbf{not} complementary the way independent sets and coverings are.
The book is explicit about this (\S{}7.1, p. 110):
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber]
\lean{SimpleGraph.indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber}
\uses{SimpleGraph.edgeCoveringNumber}
K\"onig's min-max equality transported across the two Gallai identities.  The book
introduces it with (\S{}7.1, p. 110):
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_two_mul_indepNum_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_two_mul_indepNum_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_two_mul_indepNum_le}
($\Rightarrow$) Every subgraph of a bipartite graph is bipartite, and the larger side of a
bipartition is an independent set with at least half the vertices.

($\Leftarrow$) If $G$ were not bipartite it would contain an odd cycle (Thm 1.2).  That
cycle on $2k+1$ vertices has $\alpha = k$, and $2k < 2k+1$, so the condition fails at
that subgraph.

Stated as $\nu(H) \le 2\cdot\alpha(H)$ to avoid division.

"Subgraph $H$ of $G$" is \texttt{H : G.Subgraph}, which carries its own \texttt{verts} --- so
$\nu(H)$ genuinely shrinks and the odd-cycle witness is expressible.  \texttt{H.coe} is
the subgraph viewed as a \texttt{SimpleGraph ↥H.verts}, and \texttt{H.verts.ncard} is used in
place of \texttt{Fintype.card ↥H.verts} to avoid an instance that \texttt{[Fintype V]} alone
does not supply.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber}
\uses{SimpleGraph.edgeCoveringNumber}
($\Rightarrow$) Theorem 7.3 applied subgraph-wise, every subgraph of a bipartite graph being
bipartite.

($\Leftarrow$) Contrapositive: an odd cycle $H$ on $2k+1$ vertices has $\delta(H) = 2 > 0$,
$\alpha(H) = k$ and $\beta'(H) = k + 1$, so the equality fails there.

So the identity $\alpha = \beta'$ --- which Theorem 7.3 gives for bipartite graphs ---
actually \emph{characterises} them.

\textbf{!} The instance binders \texttt{[Fintype H.verts] $\to$ [DecidableRel H.coe.Adj] $\to$} sit
\textbf{inside} the $\forall H$, as hypotheses rather than instance arguments.  That is
unusual and means a user must supply them explicitly at each application; it also
means the ($\Leftarrow$) direction gets to \emph{assume} them for its witness, which is harmless
here but worth noticing.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[$\alpha$-critical: deleting any edge raises the independence number]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsAlphaCritical}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsAlphaCritical}
\leanok
Every edge matters for $\alpha$: removing any one lets a larger independent set
appear, so an $\alpha$-critical graph has no $\alpha$-redundant edges.

$G - e$ is \texttt{G.deleteEdges \{e\}}, on the same vertex type --- so $\nu$ is unchanged,
which is what makes the equivalence with $\beta$-criticality (below) exact.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[no_cutVertex_of_isAlphaCritical]
\lean{SimpleGraph.no_cutVertex_of_isAlphaCritical}
\label{SimpleGraph.no_cutVertex_of_isAlphaCritical}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsAlphaCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
Suppose $v$ is a cut vertex, so $G - v$ splits.  Independent sets can be chosen
per component, and one shows some edge at $v$ is deletable without increasing
$\alpha$ --- contradicting criticality, where \emph{every} deletion must raise it.

So $\alpha$-criticality forces a structure that cannot be pieced together at a single
articulation point.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[$\beta$-critical: deleting any edge lowers the covering number]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsBetaCritical}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsBetaCritical}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.coveringNumber}
Every edge is essential to the covering number.

\textbf{+} By Corollary 7.1 ($\alpha + \beta = \nu$) and the fact that edge deletion leaves $\nu$
unchanged, this is \textbf{literally equivalent} to \texttt{IsAlphaCritical} --- which is why
the two exercises are parallel, and why 7.1.3(a) reduces to 7.1.2 in one line
once Cor 7.1 is available.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[no_cutVertex_of_isBetaCritical]
\lean{SimpleGraph.no_cutVertex_of_isBetaCritical}
\label{SimpleGraph.no_cutVertex_of_isBetaCritical}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsBetaCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
Corollary 7.1 gives $\alpha + \beta = \nu$ for every graph on the vertex type, and edge
deletion leaves $\nu$ fixed.  So $\beta(G - e) < \beta(G)$ $\iff$ $\alpha(G - e) > \alpha(G)$, and
$\beta$-critical is the same condition as $\alpha$-critical.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[two_mul_coveringNumber_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.two_mul_coveringNumber_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.two_mul_coveringNumber_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.coveringNumber}
Stated as $2\beta \le \varepsilon + 1$ to avoid division.

A minimum covering touches every edge, and in a connected graph the edges are
linked tightly enough that each covering vertex can be charged at least two
edges, with one left over for a spanning tree's root.

\textbf{!} Note the book states this under 7.1.3, whose preamble defines $\beta$-critical ---
but part (b) does \textbf{not} assume $\beta$-criticality, only connectivity, and the Lean
signature correctly reflects that.  (The docstring previously implied the
$\beta$-critical hypothesis carried over; it does not.)

Connectivity is essential: a disjoint union of $k$ edges has $\beta = k = \varepsilon$, which
violates the bound for $k \ge 2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound}
\leanok
\texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound}
The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without
it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[isRamseyBound_mono]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isRamseyBound_mono}
\label{SimpleGraph.isRamseyBound_mono}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound}
A bigger graph contains a smaller one: restrict a graph on $m$ vertices to any
$n$ of them, get a $k$-clique or $l$-independent set there, and it survives in
the larger graph.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists_isRamseyBound]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_isRamseyBound}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_isRamseyBound}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound}
No matter how a graph is drawn, if it is large enough it cannot avoid \emph{both} a
big clique and a big independent set.

The book can be informal about existence because $r(k,l)$ is only ever used
comparatively.  In Lean, \texttt{ramseyNumber} is \texttt{sInf} over a set that this lemma
proves nonempty --- so \textbf{until this is proved, every \texttt{ramseyNumber} in the file is
provably $0$} and every result below is vacuous.  It gates all of \S{}7.2 and, via
Schur, \S{}7.4.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The consequence every later item consumes: $r(k,l)$ really is a Ramsey bound]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isRamseyBound_ramseyNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.isRamseyBound_ramseyNumber}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound, SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
\texttt{ramseyNumber} is an \texttt{sInf}.  Once the set is nonempty (\texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound})
it contains its infimum (\texttt{Nat.sInf\_mem}), so $r(k,l)$ genuinely has the defining
property.

Note \texttt{isRamseyBound\_mono} is not needed for \emph{this} --- \texttt{Nat.sInf\_mem} alone
suffices --- but it is what makes $r(k,l)$ the sharp threshold rather than merely
\emph{a} bound.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyNumber_one_left]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_one_left}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_one_left}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
A 1-clique is a single vertex, which any nonempty graph has.  So one vertex
suffices.

\textbf{!} $n = 1$ must genuinely satisfy \texttt{IsRamseyBound 1 1 l} \textbf{and} no smaller $n$
must --- but $n = 0$ also satisfies it vacuously \emph{only if} \texttt{Fin 0} graphs have a
1-clique, which they do not.  So the \texttt{sInf} really is $1$, but the $n = 0$ case
has to be ruled out explicitly rather than assumed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyNumber_one_right]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_one_right}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_one_right}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
A 1-element independent set is a single vertex.  The mirror image of
\texttt{ramseyNumber\_one\_left}, and derivable from it via \texttt{ramseyNumber\_comm}
(Ex 7.2.1) --- though proving it directly is just as short.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyNumber_two_left]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_two_left}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_two_left}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
A 2-clique is an edge.  On $l$ vertices either some edge is present --- a
2-clique --- or there are none, and all $l$ vertices are independent.  So $l$
suffices; and $l - 1$ does not, since $\bot$ on \texttt{Fin (l-1)} has no edge and no
$l$-element independent set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyNumber_two_right]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_two_right}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_two_right}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
A 2-element independent set is a non-adjacent pair.  On $k$ vertices either some
pair is non-adjacent, or every pair is adjacent and all $k$ form a clique.  The
complete graph on $k - 1$ vertices shows $k$ is needed.

The mirror of \texttt{ramseyNumber\_two\_left} under \texttt{ramseyNumber\_comm}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramsey_recursion]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramsey_recursion}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramsey_recursion}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
The engine behind both the exact values in the book's table and the binomial
bound of Theorem 7.5.

\textbf{!} $l - 1$ and $k - 1$ are $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction; $hk$, $hl$ keep them from truncating,
but the proof must still convert $l - 1 + 1 = l$ explicitly at each use.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramsey_recursion_strict]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramsey_recursion_strict}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramsey_recursion_strict}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
The parity refinement that pins down $r(3,4) = 9$: $r(3,3) = 6$ and $r(2,4) = 4$
are both even, so $r(3,4) \le 6 + 4 - 1 = 9$.

\textbf{!} The book's "in particular, $v$ cannot be adjacent to precisely $r(k-1,l) - 1$
vertices" is the crux and compresses a parity computation: with both summands
even, $r(k-1,l) - 1$ is odd, so a vertex of even degree cannot have exactly that
degree.  That one configuration is precisely the one where neither (i) nor (ii)
holds, so ruling it out restores the case analysis.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[cycleGraph_five_cliqueFree_three]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cycleGraph_five_cliqueFree_three}
\label{SimpleGraph.cycleGraph_five_cliqueFree_three}
$C_{5}$ has girth 5, so no triangle: each vertex has two neighbours and they are not
adjacent to each other.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[cycleGraph_five_indepSetFree_three]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cycleGraph_five_indepSetFree_three}
\label{SimpleGraph.cycleGraph_five_indepSetFree_three}
Any three of five cyclic positions include two consecutive ones, hence adjacent.
So $\alpha(C_{5}) = 2$.

$C_{5}$ is self-complementary, which is what makes it work on both sides at once ---
the book conjectures (\S{}7.2, p. 114) that all $(k,k)$-Ramsey graphs are.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[six_le_ramseyNumber_three_three]
\lean{SimpleGraph.six_le_ramseyNumber_three_three}
\label{SimpleGraph.six_le_ramseyNumber_three_three}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
$C_{5}$ witnesses that five vertices do not force either structure, so the threshold
is $\ge 6$.  Combined with Thm 7.4 this is the exact value: among any six people,
three are mutual acquaintances or three mutual strangers.

\textbf{!} Only the \textbf{lower} bound is stated here; the file does not state $r(3,3) = 6$.
Same for $r(3,5)$ and $r(4,4)$ below --- all three exact values in the book's
worked examples are left unstated.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The (3,5)-Ramsey graph: \texttt{ZMod 13}, adjacent iff the difference is a cubic residue]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13}
\label{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13}
A circulant on \texttt{ZMod 13}.  ${1, 5, 8, 12}$ is closed under negation
($-1 = 12$, $-5 = 8$), which is exactly what makes \texttt{symm} hold --- so unlike most
\texttt{def}s in this repo, \texttt{symm} and \texttt{loopless} are \textbf{genuinely discharged}, by
\texttt{decide}.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, no \texttt{sorry} --- one of the few complete constructions in the
directory.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[cubicResidueGraph13_cliqueFree_three]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13_cliqueFree_three}
\label{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13_cliqueFree_three}
\uses{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13}
A triangle needs three residues pairwise differing by an element of
${1, 5, 8, 12}$; the arithmetic rules it out.  The graph is 4-regular and
triangle-free.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[cubicResidueGraph13_indepSetFree_five]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13_indepSetFree_five}
\label{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13_indepSetFree_five}
\uses{SimpleGraph.cubicResidueGraph13}
Five pairwise non-adjacent vertices would be five residues no two differing by an
element of ${1, 5, 8, 12}$.  With thirteen residues and four forbidden
differences, no such set exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[fourteen_le_ramseyNumber_three_five]
\lean{SimpleGraph.fourteen_le_ramseyNumber_three_five}
\label{SimpleGraph.fourteen_le_ramseyNumber_three_five}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
Thirteen vertices do not suffice, so the threshold is $\ge 14$.

\textbf{!} The book's upper bound chain routes through $r(3,4) = 9$, which itself needs
the \textbf{strict} form of Theorem 7.4 ($r(3,3)$ and $r(2,4)$ both even).  Neither
$r(3,4) = 9$ nor its ingredients are stated in this file, so the exact value
$r(3,5) = 14$ is not reachable from what is here even once everything is proved.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The (4,4)-Ramsey graph = the Paley graph of order 17]
\lean{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17}
\label{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17}
The \textbf{Paley graph} of order 17 --- the canonical self-complementary, highly
symmetric graph.  ${1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16}$ is closed under negation
($-1 = 16$, $-2 = 15$, \dots), so \texttt{symm} holds.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, \texttt{symm}/\texttt{loopless} discharged by \texttt{decide} --- no \texttt{sorry}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[paleyGraph17_cliqueFree_four]
\lean{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17_cliqueFree_four}
\label{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17_cliqueFree_four}
\uses{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17}
Four vertices pairwise differing by quadratic residues would be a $K_{4}$; the
arithmetic of ${1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16}$ prevents it, so $\omega = 3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[paleyGraph17_indepSetFree_four]
\lean{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17_indepSetFree_four}
\label{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17_indepSetFree_four}
\uses{SimpleGraph.paleyGraph17}
\textbf{+} \textbf{The slick route}: the Paley graph of order 17 is self-complementary (the
book notes this), so a 4-element independent set would be a $K_{4}$ in the
complement, i.e. in an isomorphic copy --- ruled out by the previous lemma.

\textbf{!} But that route costs a self-complementarity proof (an explicit isomorphism
$x \mapsto gx$ for $g$ a non-residue), which is more work than the direct check.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[eighteen_le_ramseyNumber_four_four]
\lean{SimpleGraph.eighteen_le_ramseyNumber_four_four}
\label{SimpleGraph.eighteen_le_ramseyNumber_four_four}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
Seventeen vertices do not suffice, so the threshold is $\ge 18$ --- and with the
upper bound, exactly $18$, the largest value in the book's table.

\textbf{!} As with $r(3,5)$, only the lower bound is stated here, and the upper bound
would need $r(3,4) = 9$ --- itself unstated and requiring the strict form of
Theorem 7.4.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyNumber_le_choose]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_le_choose}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_le_choose}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
$r(k, l) \le C(k + l - 2, k - 1)$.

Theorem 7.4's recursion is exactly Pascal's rule, so the Ramsey numbers are
dominated by binomial coefficients.  Setting $k = l$ gives roughly $r(k,k) \le 4^k$;
Theorem 7.6 gives $2^{k/2}$ below, and closing that gap is still open.

\textbf{!} Three $\mathbb{N}$ subtractions in the statement ($k + l - 2$, $k - 1$, and $m - 2$ in the
proof).  The Pascal step $C(m+n-3, m-1) + C(m+n-3, m-2) = C(m+n-2, m-1)$ is
\texttt{Nat.choose\_succ\_succ} only after the indices are massaged into \texttt{succ} form ---
budget for that.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[card_simpleGraph_fin]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_simpleGraph_fin}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_simpleGraph_fin}
A simple graph on a labelled vertex set is determined by which of the $C(n,2)$
possible edges are present.

\textbf{!} Mathlib has a \texttt{Fintype (SimpleGraph (Fin n))} instance but \textbf{no cardinality
lemma}, so this genuinely has to be proved.  The route is an equiv
\texttt{SimpleGraph (Fin n) $\simeq$ (Sym2 (Fin n) \textbackslash\{\} diagonal $\to$ Bool)}, or via
\texttt{Finset.powerset} on the non-diagonal \texttt{Sym2}s --- the \texttt{Sym2} bookkeeping is the
work, not the arithmetic.

The counting fact underlying Erd\H{o}s' probabilistic proof of Theorem 7.6.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramsey_self_lower_bound]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramsey_self_lower_bound}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramsey_self_lower_bound}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
The \textbf{probabilistic method}, which the book introduces as (\S{}7.2, p. 115):

The exponent $k/2$ is real, hence the $\mathbb{R}$-valued statement --- the one place in
this chapter where $\mathbb{N}$ will not do.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyNumber_ge_of_min]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_ge_of_min}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_ge_of_min}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
Ramsey numbers are monotone in both arguments, so $r(k,l) \ge r(m,m)$ for
\texttt{m = min(k,l)}; then Theorem 7.6.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Monotonicity of \texttt{ramseyNumber} in its arguments is not stated in this file.}
\texttt{isRamseyBound\_mono} is monotonicity in $n$, a different thing.  The needed
lemma --- $k \le k' \to l \le l' \to r(k,l) \le r(k',l')$ --- has to be added; it follows from
\texttt{IsRamseyBound n k' l' $\to$ IsRamseyBound n k l} (a bigger clique contains a
smaller one).
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[An $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$: a total function on unordered pairs]
\lean{SimpleGraph.EdgeColouring}
\label{SimpleGraph.EdgeColouring}
\leanok
A total function \texttt{Sym2 (Fin n) $\to$ Fin m} --- colouring every pair, including the
diagonal, which is harmless since \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti} only inspects $s(u,v)$ for
$u \ne v$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} Mathlib's \texttt{SimpleGraph.Coloring}, which colours \emph{vertices}.  Also not
chapter 6's \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, which is partial (defined only on actual edges);
here the host graph is $K_{n}$, so every pair is an edge and a total function is
right.

"One easily sees" that the two formulations agree for $m = 2$ --- but this file
\textbf{does not state that equivalence}, so \texttt{ramseyNumber} and \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti} at
$m = 2$ are formally unrelated.  Anything wanting to move between \S{}7.2's two
halves needs that bridge.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}: every $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$ has, for some $i$, a set of $c i$\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBoundMulti}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBoundMulti}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.EdgeColouring}
Colour every pair of $n$ points with one of $m$ colours; once $n$ is large
enough, some colour $i$ covers all edges within some $k_{i}$ points.

The target sizes are a function \texttt{c : Fin m $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$} rather than a list, which makes
\texttt{Function.update c i (c i - 1)} the natural way to express "decrement the $i$-th
argument" in Theorem 7.7 below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The multicolour Ramsey number $r(k_{1},\dots,k_m)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumberMulti}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumberMulti}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBoundMulti}
\textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap as \texttt{ramseyNumber}, and \textbf{worse}: there is no
\texttt{exists\_isRamseyBoundMulti} anywhere in the file.  So every \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}
is provably $0$ as things stand, which makes \texttt{ramseyMulti\_recursion},
\texttt{ramseyTriangle\_*} and Schur's theorem in \S{}7.4 all vacuous.

With $m = 2$ this should reduce to \texttt{ramseyNumber}, but that bridge is unstated
(see \texttt{EdgeColouring}).

$k_{1} = \dots = k_m = 3$ gives the sequence $r_{n}$ of exercise 7.2.3, which is what
Schur's theorem consumes in \S{}7.4.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyMulti_recursion]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyMulti_recursion}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyMulti_recursion}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumberMulti}
Generalises Theorem 7.4's recursion.  Fix $v$ in a large $K_{n}$ and classify the
other vertices by the colour of their edge to $v$.  If every colour class were
smaller than $r(\dots, k_{i}-1, \dots)$, the classes could not cover all vertices --- which is
exactly what the bound arranges.  Some class is then big enough for a
monochromatic complete subgraph, and $v$ extends it in colour $i$.

Stated additively ($+ m$ on the left, $+ 2$ on the right) to avoid the $\mathbb{N}$
subtraction $- m + 2$.

\textbf{!} \texttt{Function.update c i (c i - 1)} still has an inner $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction; $hc : \forall i, 2 \le c i$
keeps it from truncating.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyMulti_le_multinomial]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyMulti_le_multinomial}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyMulti_le_multinomial}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumberMulti}
Iterating Theorem 7.7 gives exactly the multinomial recursion, as the two-colour
case gave binomials in Theorem 7.5.

With $m = 2$ this is Theorem 7.5, since $(k_{1}+k_{2})!/(k_{1}!k_{2}!) = C(k_{1}+k_{2}, k_{1})$.

\textbf{!} The division is exact but is $\mathbb{N}$ division in Lean; as with \texttt{card\_perfectMatching\_completeGraph}
in chapter 5, the proof should establish the \emph{multiplied} form
$r(\dots) * \prod k_{i}! \le (\sum k_{i})!$ and divide only at the end.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyNumber_comm]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_comm}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber_comm}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
Complementation swaps cliques and independent sets, so a graph with no $k$-clique
and no $l$-independent set becomes one with no $l$-clique and no $k$-independent
set.  The thresholds coincide.

Why the book's table is symmetric about its diagonal.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[$r_{n} = r(3, \dots, 3)$ with $n$ colours]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumberMulti}
The least number of points such that any $n$-colouring of the pairs forces a
monochromatic \emph{triangle}.  $r_{2} = r(3,3) = 6$; Greenwood and Gleason showed
$r_{3} = 17$.

Exactly what Schur's theorem (\S{}7.4) consumes.

\textbf{!} Inherits \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}'s missing existence lemma, so \texttt{ramseyTriangle n}
is currently provably $0$ for every $n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyTriangle_recursion]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle_recursion}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle_recursion}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle}
Theorem 7.7 with all targets $3$.  Fix $v$ in a $K_{n}$ on $n(r_{n-1}-1) + 2$
vertices; its $n(r_{n-1}-1) + 1$ neighbours split among $n$ colours, so some
class has $\ge r_{n-1}$ vertices.  Either two of them are joined in that same
colour --- a monochromatic triangle with $v$ --- or the class avoids that colour and
its induced colouring uses only $n-1$ colours, where $r_{n-1}$ vertices force a
triangle.

Stated additively ($+ n$ on the left) to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyTriangle_le_factorial_exp]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle_le_factorial_exp}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle_le_factorial_exp}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle}
Unwinding $r_{n} \le n(r_{n-1} - 1) + 2$ from $r_{2} = 6$ and dividing by $n!$ gives a
telescoping sum of reciprocals $1/k!$, which converge to $e$.  Hence
$r_{n} - 1 \le n! e$.

$e$ appears precisely as $\sum 1/k!$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyTriangle_three_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle_three_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle_three_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle}
Part (a) at $n = 3$ with $r_{2} = 6$: $r_{3} \le 3(6-1) + 2 = 17$.  (Part (b) also gives
$\lfloor 6e\rfloor + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17$.)

So among any seventeen points, any 3-colouring of the pairs forces a
monochromatic triangle.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The composition (lexicographic product) $G(H)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.composition}
\label{SimpleGraph.composition}
Replace each vertex of $G$ by a copy of $H$.  Vertices in \emph{different} copies are
joined iff the corresponding $G$-vertices are adjacent; within one copy, iff
adjacent in $H$.  The $G$-structure dominates --- hence the alternative name
\emph{lexicographic product}.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, \texttt{symm} and \texttt{loopless} both discharged --- no \texttt{sorry}.

\textbf{!} Distinct from chapter 6's \texttt{boxProd} ($G \square H$), where within-copy and
across-copy edges are treated symmetrically.  Composition is not commutative.

Parts (b) and (c) of the exercise, to multiply Ramsey lower bounds.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[indepNum_composition_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.indepNum_composition_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.indepNum_composition_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.composition}
Let $S$ be independent in $G[H]$.  Its first-coordinate projection is independent
in $G$ (two $S$-vertices in different copies force those $G$-vertices
non-adjacent), so at most $\alpha(G)$ copies are touched; within each, at most $\alpha(H)$
vertices.  Multiply.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramsey_product_lower]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramsey_product_lower}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramsey_product_lower}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
Take $(k+1,k+1)$- and $(l+1,l+1)$-Ramsey graphs $G$, $H$ --- so $\omega, \alpha \le k$ and
$\le l$ respectively --- and form $G[H]$, which has the product vertex count.  Part
(a) gives $\alpha(G[H]) \le kl$; complementing gives $\omega(G[H]) \le kl$.  So $G[H]$ avoids
both a $(kl+1)$-clique and a $(kl+1)$-independent set.

Stated additively ($\dots + 1 \le r(\dots)$) to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction on the outside --- though
the two inner $- 1$s remain.

\textbf{!} The complement step needs $(G[H])^{c} \cong G^{c}[H^{c}]$, which is \textbf{true but not
obvious} and is not stated in this file.  Without it, part (a) bounds only $\alpha$
and the clique side has to be argued separately.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[abbott_lower_bound]
\lean{SimpleGraph.abbott_lower_bound}
\label{SimpleGraph.abbott_lower_bound}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
Iterate part (b) from $r(3,3) = 6$, so $r(3,3) - 1 = 5$.  Taking $k = l = 2^{n-1}$
each step multiplies by $5$.  The witness is the $n$-fold composition of $C_{5}$
with itself.

The best \textbf{constructive} bound, versus Corollary 7.6's probabilistic one.  With
$k = 2^{n}$, \texttt{5$^{n}$ = k\^{}\{log$_{2}$5\} $\approx$ k\^{}\{2.32\}} is merely polynomial in $k$, while $2^{k/2}$
is exponential --- the gap the book remarks on.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[$C_{3} \lor C_{5}$ on the carrier \texttt{Fin 3 $\oplus$ Fin 5}]
\lean{SimpleGraph.grahamGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.grahamGraph}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.join}
$C_{3} \lor C_{5}$ on \texttt{Fin 3 $\oplus$ Fin 5}: two disjoint cycles with every vertex of one joined
to every vertex of the other, on $8$ vertices.

A \emph{small} graph with no $K_{6}$ in which every 2-edge colouring still forces a
monochromatic triangle --- so "contains $K_{6}$" is not necessary for the Ramsey
property.

\textbf{+} An \texttt{abbrev} built from \texttt{join} and \texttt{cycleGraph}, fully defined.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The generalised Ramsey number $r(G_{1},\dots,G_m)$ over Mathlib's containment $\sqsubseteq$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
\leanok
Instead of a monochromatic \emph{complete} subgraph, a monochromatic copy of a
prescribed graph.  All $G_{i}$ complete recovers \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}.

"Subgraph isomorphic to $G_{i}$" is Mathlib's containment $\sqsubseteq$, and the colour-$i$
graph is \texttt{fromEdgeSet \{e | $\chi$ e = i $\land$ $\lnot$ e.IsDiag\}} --- the \texttt{$\lnot$ IsDiag} guard being
what stops the diagonal from creating spurious loops.

\textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap again, with \textbf{no} existence lemma for this notion
either.  So all four generalised-Ramsey results below are vacuous as stated.

\textbf{!} The graphs are indexed by \texttt{W : Fin m $\to$ Type*}, so each $G_{i}$ may live on a
different carrier --- flexible, but it means \texttt{![pathGraph 4, pathGraph 4]} below
must elaborate its motive carefully.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[tree_isContained_of_minDegree_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.tree_isContained_of_minDegree_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.tree_isContained_of_minDegree_le}
\emph{ (absent from Mathlib).  }If $\delta(G) \ge m - 1$
then every tree $T$ on $m$ vertices embeds in $G$.*

Build the embedding greedily.  A tree on $m$ vertices can be listed so each new
vertex attaches to exactly one already-placed vertex (peel leaves).  Placing the
$j$-th, its unique placed neighbour has $\ge m - 1$ neighbours in $G$, of which at
most $j - 1 \le m - 2$ are used --- a fresh image always exists.

The standard "minimum degree forces every small tree" lemma; it is what makes
tree-target Ramsey numbers exactly computable.

\textbf{!} $m$ is a free variable in the signature, tied to $W$ only through
\texttt{hm : Fintype.card W = m} --- so $m$ is determined but Lean will not infer it;
callers must supply it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[generalisedRamsey_tree_star]
\lean{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamsey_tree_star}
\label{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamsey_tree_star}
\uses{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
$K_{1,n}$ is the \textbf{star} with $n$ leaves, so a blue copy is a vertex with $n$
blue edges.  On $m + n - 1$ points, if no vertex has $n$ blue edges then every
vertex has $\ge (m+n-2) - (n-1) = m - 1$ red edges, and
\texttt{tree\_isContained\_of\_minDegree\_le} embeds $T$ in red.

Lower bound: a colouring of $K_{m+n-2}$ with no red $T$ and no blue star.  The
divisibility $(m-1) \mid (n-1)$ is exactly what lets the red graph be
$(m-2)$-regular --- too sparse for $T$, while leaving every vertex under $n$ blue
edges.

\textbf{!} The two targets live on \textbf{different carriers} ($W$ and \texttt{Fin 1 $\oplus$ Fin n}), so
$![T, K_{1,n}]$ cannot elaborate --- \texttt{Matrix.vecCons} is homogeneous.  Hence the
dependent spelling \texttt{Fin.cons T (Fin.cons \_ finZeroElim)} with an explicit type
family \texttt{W := ![W, Fin 1 $\oplus$ Fin n]}, and \texttt{W : Type} rather than \texttt{Type*}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[chvatal_tree_complete]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_tree_complete}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_tree_complete}
\uses{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
One of the cleanest results in generalised Ramsey theory: the answer depends on
the tree only through its \textbf{number of vertices}, not its shape.

\emph{Lower bound.}  Partition $(m-1)(n-1)$ points into $n-1$ groups of $m-1$; red
inside groups, blue between.  Red is a disjoint union of $K_{m-1}$s, too small
for a tree on $m$ vertices; blue is complete $(n-1)$-partite, so its largest
clique has $n-1$ vertices --- no $K_{n}$.

\emph{Upper bound.}  On $(m-1)(n-1) + 1$ points, if blue has no $K_{n}$ then Tur\'an-type
reasoning gives red minimum degree $\ge m-1$ somewhere, and the sub-lemma embeds
$T$.

\textbf{!} Same heterogeneous-carrier spelling as part (b).

\textbf{!} The upper bound's "Tur\'an-type reasoning" is genuinely \S{}7.3's Theorem 7.9 ---
so this exercise depends on the \emph{next} section, not just on \S{}7.2.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[degreeMajorised_of_cliqueFree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.degreeMajorised_of_cliqueFree}
\label{SimpleGraph.degreeMajorised_of_cliqueFree}
\uses{SimpleGraph.DegreeMajorised, SimpleGraph.degreeSequence}
The book remarks (\S{}7.3, p. 118) on the parallel with Theorem 4.6:

\textbf{!} \textbf{Blocked on \texttt{degreeSequence} being unsorted} --- see the warning there.  The
book's \texttt{DegreeMajorised} compares \emph{nondecreasing} sequences; against this file's
unsorted list the predicate is not even isomorphism-invariant, so the equality
clause (\texttt{same degree sequence $\to$ G $\cong$ H}) cannot be right as stated.  Fix
\texttt{degreeSequence} first.

\textbf{!} The carrier changes: $H$ is existentially quantified over a fresh type $W$, so
\texttt{DegreeMajorised G H} compares across types via the \texttt{Fintype.card V = Fintype.card W}
conjunct.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[degreeMajorised_of_forall_degree_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.degreeMajorised_of_forall_degree_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.degreeMajorised_of_forall_degree_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.DegreeMajorised}
(absent from Mathlib).  *If $d_G(v) \le d_H(v)$ for
every vertex $v$, then $G$ is degree-majorised by $H$.*

Degree-majorisation compares \emph{sorted} sequences entrywise.  Pointwise domination
survives sorting: the $i$-th smallest degree of $G$ cannot exceed the $i$-th
smallest of $H$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Two problems with this as stated.}

1. \texttt{degreeSequence} in this file is \textbf{unsorted}, so "sorting preserves
   domination" is not what the predicate says --- the entrywise comparison is
   against \texttt{Finset.univ.toList}'s arbitrary order.  With both graphs on the same
   $V$ that order is at least \emph{the same} on both sides, so pointwise domination
   does happen to give the conclusion --- but only by accident of the shared
   carrier, not because the lemma is right.
2. It is stated for \texttt{G H : SimpleGraph V} on the \textbf{same} carrier, whereas
   Theorem 7.8 needs it across different carriers ($G$ on $V$, $H$ on $W$).  So
   it does not actually discharge the step it was extracted for.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[turan_iso_of_card_edgeFinset_eq]
\lean{SimpleGraph.turan_iso_of_card_edgeFinset_eq}
\label{SimpleGraph.turan_iso_of_card_edgeFinset_eq}
The balanced complete multipartite graph is not merely \emph{an} extremal example but
the \textbf{unique} one, up to isomorphism.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[triangle_of_card_edgeFinset_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.triangle_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.triangle_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
Tur\'an at $m = 2$ --- Mantel's 1907 case, half a century before the
generalisation.  Extremal example: balanced $K_{\lfloor\nu/2\rfloor,\lceil\nu/2\rceil}$ with $\lfloor\nu^{2}/4\rfloor$
edges.

Cleared to $\nu^{2} < 4\varepsilon$ to avoid division.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[triangle_of_not_bipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.triangle_of_not_bipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.triangle_of_not_bipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
Forbidding bipartiteness on top of triangle-freeness drops the cap from $\nu^{2}/4$ to
$(\nu-1)^{2}/4 + 1$.  A triangle-free non-bipartite graph contains an odd cycle of
length $\ge 5$, which is an inefficient use of vertices; the densest such graph is
essentially $C_{5}$ blown up.

The \textbf{stability} phenomenon of extremal graph theory: near-extremal graphs all
resemble the extremal one, so departing from it costs edges.

Cleared to $(\nu-1)^{2} + 4 < 4\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_sum_choose_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_sum_choose_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_sum_choose_gt}
Double-count \textbf{cherries} (paths of length two).  Each $v$ centres $C(d(v),2)$ of
them, so the total is $\sum_v C(d(v),2)$; each is determined by its two \emph{endpoints},
an unordered pair from $C(\nu,2)$.  If no pair had $m$ common neighbours, each pair
would host $\le m-1$ cherries, capping the total at $(m-1)C(\nu,2)$.

The prototype for K\H{o}v\'ari--S\'os--Tur\'an (exercise 7.3.5).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_card_edgeFinset_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
Convert part (a)'s degree condition into an edge count.  By convexity,
$\sum_v C(d(v),2)$ is minimised at fixed $\varepsilon$ when all degrees equal $2\varepsilon/\nu$, so
$\sum_v C(d(v),2) \ge \nu \cdot C(2\varepsilon/\nu, 2)$; demanding this exceed $(m-1)C(\nu,2)$ and solving
for $\varepsilon$ gives the threshold.

A genuinely \textbf{sub-quadratic} threshold ($\nu^{3/2}$), unlike Tur\'an's for cliques.

\textbf{!} Real-valued with \texttt{rpow} exponents, so the proof leaves $\mathbb{N}$ early.  Mathlib's
\texttt{inner\_mul\_le\_norm\_mul\_norm} or \texttt{Finset.inner\_mul\_le\_norm\_mul\_norm} /
\texttt{sq\_sum\_le\_card\_mul\_sum\_sq} supply the convexity step; \texttt{Finset.inner\_card\_le\_...}
is the usual shape for "sum of $C(d_{v},2)$ versus the average".
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The unit-distance graph on a finite point set in the plane]
\lean{SimpleGraph.unitDistanceGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.unitDistanceGraph}
Join $i, j$ when \texttt{dist (x i) (x j) = 1}.  Carrier \texttt{EuclideanSpace $\mathbb{R}$ (Fin 2)}.

The geometry enters as a forbidden subgraph: two points have at most \textbf{two}
common unit-distance neighbours (two unit circles meet in $\le$ 2 points), so the
graph has no $K_{2,3}$, and 7.3.4(b) bounds $\varepsilon$.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, \texttt{symm} and \texttt{loopless} both discharged --- no \texttt{sorry}.

\textbf{!} The $i \ne j$ conjunct in \texttt{Adj} is doing real work: without it, \texttt{dist (x i) (x i)
= 0 $\ne$ 1} would still exclude loops, but only if the $x i$ are \emph{distinct points}.
Since $x$ is not assumed injective, two indices may carry the same point, and
$i \ne j$ is what keeps the graph simple in that case.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[card_unit_distance_pairs_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_unit_distance_pairs_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_unit_distance_pairs_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.unitDistanceGraph}
Two distinct points have $\le 2$ common unit-distance neighbours (two unit circles
meet in $\le 2$ points), so the graph is $K_{2,3}$-free; 7.3.4(b) at $m = 3$ gives
$\varepsilon \le (\sqrt 2 \cdot n^{3/2})/2 + n/4 = n^{3/2}/\sqrt 2 + n/4$.

A purely combinatorial bound on a geometric quantity, obtained by turning a fact
about circles into a forbidden subgraph.  The true order of growth of the
unit-distance problem is still open (Erd\H{o}s).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isContained_completeBipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
Generalises 7.3.4 from $K_{2,m}$ to $K_{m,m}$.  Count \emph{stars} --- a vertex with $m$
of its neighbours --- two ways: each $v$ contributes $C(d(v), m)$, and each
$m$-set can be the leaf-set of $\le m-1$ stars unless a $K_{m,m}$ appears.
Convexity converts the degree sum into an edge count.

The exponent $2 - 1/m$ is the point: forbidding a complete \emph{bipartite} subgraph
caps $\varepsilon$ at strictly sub-quadratic order, unlike Tur\'an's constant fraction of
$\nu^{2}$.  Whether the exponent is tight for every $m$ is the \textbf{Zarankiewicz
problem}, still open.

\textbf{!} The \texttt{rpow} exponent varies with $m$, so this is irreducibly real-valued; and
$(m - 1 : \mathbb{R})$ with $hm : 1 \le m$ means the base can be $0$ at $m = 1$, where
$0 ^ (1/1) = 0$ --- check that boundary case does not make the hypothesis vacuous.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[schur]
\lean{SimpleGraph.schur}
\label{SimpleGraph.schur}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyTriangle}
The classical bridge from Ramsey theory to additive number theory.  Schur's
original motivation was Fermat's Last Theorem mod $p$.

The book's motivating example (\S{}7.4, p. 120):

\textbf{!} Note "not necessarily distinct" --- so $x = y$ is allowed, and the Lean statement
correctly does not require distinctness.

\textbf{!} \texttt{hpart} says every $k \in [1, r_{n}]$ lies in exactly one part, and \texttt{hsub} that no
part escapes the range --- together a genuine partition.  But \textbf{nothing forces the
parts nonempty}, which is fine (empty parts are harmless).
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The Schur number $s_{n}$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.schurNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.schurNumber}
\leanok
The exact threshold at which sum-free partitions become impossible.

\textbf{+} Unlike most \texttt{sInf}s in this chapter, nonemptiness here is supplied by \textbf{Theorem
7.10} ($s_{n} \le r_{n}$) --- so \texttt{schurNumber} is well defined as soon as Schur's theorem
is, without a separate existence lemma.

\textbf{!} But that inherits Theorem 7.10's own vacuity: while \texttt{ramseyTriangle n = 0},
Theorem 7.10 gives nothing and \texttt{schurNumber} falls back to \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[schurNumber_three]
\lean{SimpleGraph.schurNumber_three}
\label{SimpleGraph.schurNumber_three}
\uses{SimpleGraph.schurNumber}
Lower bound from the book's opening partition
$({1,4,10,13}, {2,3,11,12}, {5,6,7,8,9})$ of ${1,\dots,13}$.

Compare $s_{3} \le r_{3} = 17$: the Schur number is strictly below the Ramsey number it
is derived from, so Theorem 7.10's bound is not tight.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[schurNumber_recursion]
\lean{SimpleGraph.schurNumber_recursion}
\label{SimpleGraph.schurNumber_recursion}
\uses{SimpleGraph.schurNumber}
From a sum-free $(n-1)$-partition of ${1,\dots,s_{n-1}-1}$, build an $n$-partition of
a roughly three-times-longer interval by scaling: keep the old parts tripled, and
give the new $n$-th part the leftover residues.

Stated additively as $3s_{n-1} \le s_{n} + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[schurNumber_lower_bound]
\lean{SimpleGraph.schurNumber_lower_bound}
\label{SimpleGraph.schurNumber_lower_bound}
\uses{SimpleGraph.schurNumber}
Iterate $s_{n} \ge 3s_{n-1} - 1$ from $s_{3} = 14$; solving the linear recurrence gives
$s_{n} \ge (27\cdot 3^{n-3} + 1)/2$.

Cleared to $27\cdot 3^{n-3} + 1 \le 2s_{n}$.

Schur numbers grow at least exponentially with ratio $3$; the upper bound
$s_{n} \le r_{n} \le \lfloor n!e\rfloor + 1$ grows factorially, and the true rate is unknown.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The "far pairs" graph: adjacent iff distance exceeds $1/\sqrt 2$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.farGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.farGraph}
\leanok
Join two points when they are "far apart", threshold $1/\sqrt 2$.  The geometry then
forbids $K_{4}$, which is what lets Tur\'an bound the number of far pairs.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, \texttt{symm}/\texttt{loopless} discharged.

\textbf{!} Same $i \ne j$ guard as \texttt{unitDistanceGraph}, and for the same reason: $x$ is not
assumed injective.

\textbf{!} The book warns (\S{}7.5, p. 121) that its "diameter" is geometric, not
graph-theoretic:

\begin{theorem}[card_farGraph_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_farGraph_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_farGraph_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.farGraph}
Two genuinely geometric inputs, neither in Mathlib:
1. \textbf{Any four points in the plane determine an angle $\ge 90^{\circ}$} --- a convex-hull
   case analysis (line / triangle / quadrilateral).
2. \textbf{The law of cosines consequence}: an angle $\ge 90^{\circ}$ at $x_{j}$ with both
   adjacent sides $> 1/\sqrt 2$ forces the opposite side $> 1$.

Given those, \texttt{farGraph} is $K_{4}$-free and \texttt{turan\_edge\_bound} at $m = 3$ finishes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists_farGraph_card_eq]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_farGraph_card_eq}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_farGraph_card_eq}
\uses{SimpleGraph.farGraph}
The far-pairs graph of this configuration is \emph{exactly} the balanced complete
tripartite $T_{3,n}$, with $\lfloor n^{2}/3\rfloor$ edges --- so the Tur\'an bound is attained and
the geometric optimum is realised by the graph-theoretic extremal configuration.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[card_unitDistanceGraph_le_of_diam_one]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_unitDistanceGraph_le_of_diam_one}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_unitDistanceGraph_le_of_diam_one}
\uses{SimpleGraph.unitDistanceGraph}
In a diameter-1 set, a pair at distance exactly $1$ is a \emph{diameter pair}.  The
key geometric fact: two diameter pairs must cross or share a point --- if $ab$ and
$cd$ were disjoint diameters, one of the four cross distances would exceed $1$.

That crossing property forces the diameter graph to have $\le n$ edges.

Contrast exercise 7.3.4(c), where without the diameter restriction the bound is
of order $n^{3/2}$; bounding the diameter collapses it to \textbf{linear}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The radio-range graph: adjacent iff within \texttt{range}]
\lean{SimpleGraph.radioGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.radioGraph}
\leanok
Join two cars when within \texttt{range}.  Turns a communications question into a degree
question: "car $i$ reaches $k$ others" is "vertex $i$ has degree $k$".

\textbf{+} Fully defined.

\textbf{!} Uses \texttt{$\le$ range}, not $<$ --- so cars at exactly the limit \emph{can} communicate.  The
exercise does not say which, and the conclusion is unaffected.
\end{definition}
